The post Access isn’t enough: why universities must make the hidden curriculum visible appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Imran Mir Programme Lead and Campus Head at Apex College Leicester and Senior Fellow of the Higher Education Academy.

Widening participation has resulted in massive improvements in the higher education sector – students from underrepresented backgrounds are entering higher education in greater numbers. This is due, in part, to decades of promotion of outreach, contextual admissions and access initiatives. Office for Students data show that, in 2023/24, 24.9% of full-time undergraduate entrants came from the most deprived areas of England, measured using Index of Multiple Deprivation quintile 1. This compared with 18.5% of entrants from the least deprived areas, measured using quintile 5.

Yet access only tells us part of the story.

The OfS data also show that inequalities still exist throughout the student lifecycle. Students from the most deprived backgrounds have a continuation rate of 83.8%, whilst students from the least deprived backgrounds have a continuation rate of 93.1%. Completion rates have shown a similar divide: 81.8% of the most deprived students complete their studies, compared with 92.7% from least deprived backgrounds. Once learners graduate, inequalities still exist. Only 66.5% of graduates from the most deprived backgrounds progress into professional employment, further study or another positive outcome within 15 months, in comparison with 74.7% of graduates from the least deprived backgrounds. These figures show that widening participation cannot just be measured solely by who enters university, but who succeeds when they are there.

The question is why.

Much attention is predominantly focused on financial hardship, wellbeing and academic preparedness – these are undoubtedly very important factors. However, there is one area which receives very little attention despite being a major element when it comes to shaping students’ everyday experiences: the hidden curriculum.

The hidden curriculum consists of the unwritten expectations, behaviours and cultural norms which students are expected to understand without actually being taught. How to approach lecturers during office hours, interpret assessment feedback, participate more confidently in seminars, build professional networks or ask for further support are sometimes seen as common knowledge when instead they are learned skills.

For some of these students, these expectations feel intuitive because they have encountered this before through family, school or social networks. Others who arrive with equal academic ability but without the same understanding of university culture.

This is not a deficit in students. It is a lack of institutional transparency.

The sociologist Pierre Bourdieu described this difference as cultural capital: the knowledge, experiences and behaviours that allow individuals to navigate institutions successfully. Universities frequently reward this familiarity without sufficiently recognising that it is unequally distributed. Confidence is often interpreted as capability, while uncertainty is mistaken for a lack of potential.

The consequences can be seen in the sector’s own data. Office for Students analysis highlighted a 17.9 percentage-point gap in achieving a first or upper second-class degree between students from the most deprived and least deprived backgrounds. Ethnicity gaps also remain substantial. In 2023/24, 80.3% of White full-time first-degree qualifiers achieved a first or 2:1 compared with 59.9% of Black full-time first-degree qualifiers. These differences cannot be explained solely by talent or effort. They point towards structural barriers that continue long after students have crossed the admissions threshold.

The hidden curriculum is very relevant when it comes to first-generation students, commuter students, mature learners and care-experienced students, who perhaps have had fewer opportunities in order to develop institutional knowledge before they arrive at university. There are also additional challenges which are faced by many neurodivergent learners. Expectations around professional communication, interpreting ambiguous instructions or navigating informal academic relationships often rely upon unwritten social conventions. When these expectations remain implicit, students who think or communicate differently are disadvantaged before teaching has even begun.

This is why I believe the sector should rethink its conversation about belonging.

Belonging has become an important priority within higher education policy, and rightly so. Students who feel connected to their institution are more likely to engage, persist and succeed. Yet belonging is rarely created by welcome weeks or social events alone. Belonging is often the result of understanding how an institution works.

The latest HEPI and Advance HE Student Academic Experience Survey, which gathered the views of more than 10,000 undergraduate students, has shown a positive picture of teaching quality and student satisfaction in spite of the financial pressures that exist. At the same time, the 2026 survey has also shown that 65% of students undertake paid work during term time, highlighting the competing demands which learners face. These realities make it more imperative for universities to reduce unnecessary barriers which exist rather than expecting students to decode institutional expectations independently.

Making the hidden curriculum visible does not mean lowering standards. It means making expectations explicit.

Universities should teach academic conventions rather than assuming prior knowledge. Assessment criteria should be unpacked through authentic examples. Professional communication, office hours and feedback should be explained as part of the curriculum rather than left to chance. Peer mentoring should focus not only on academic content but also on helping students understand how university works. Induction should become an ongoing developmental process embedded throughout the student journey rather than a single week of information at the beginning of first year.

These changes benefit everyone. The principles underpinning Universal Design for Learning remind us that when learning environments become clearer and more transparent for those facing the greatest barriers, all students gain.

Universities have worked hard to widen participation. The next challenge is ensuring they widen understanding too.

If we continue to judge students against rules we have never explicitly taught, we risk confusing confidence with competence and familiarity with potential. Equality of opportunity will not be achieved simply by opening university doors. It will be achieved when every student understands the expectations behind them.

full_text:
Rose Tremain’s autobiographical short story, inspired by an escapade from her own boarding school days, has been transformed into an extremely funny, charming and tremendously well-acted comedy written by Miriam Battye and directed by Molly Manners, all about sex, class, friendship and the awful encroachment of adulthood. As well as everything else, it refuses the glib happy ending of the traditional coming-of-age movie.

Newcomers Marni Duggan and Galaxie Clear give cracking performances as Flic and Minna, two year-10 girls and best friends for ever at a private school. They are not outsiders or emo losers; both are good at the brutal sport of lacrosse. Intent on raising their profile in advance of an attempt at Oxbridge, they audition for a production of A Midsummer Night’s Dream, which involves boys from a neighbouring school.

But they also capriciously decide that, like Titania and Bottom, they will “fall in love” with the first person they see after removing their blindfolds – this being unmarried geography teacher Miss Delavigne (Alice Englert), whom they wheedle into giving them “extra geography” at her private cabin on school grounds. The title, incidentally, also hints at a bold expansion of their own emotional territory. They are playing with fire.

This film supplies the laughs and the heartbreak and the insight that I blasphemously felt was missing from Alan Bennett’s The History Boys, although, like that oddly contrived film, this could just as well be happening 10 or 20 or even 40 years ago. The terrible injustice of that adult life for which they are so impatient is revealed to the two girls after the audition in which Minna was terrible and Flic was quite good; it is Minna who gets the lead, perhaps because of her specious blondeness, while Flic is given a humiliating non-speaking part, which compounds her unease at being a less well-off “scholarship” girl. As Minna looks like getting off with the insufferable boy playing Oberon, a terrible division begins to open between the girls.

Extra Geography recalls the wit and wisdom of Olivia Wilde’s Booksmart and Amy Heckerling’s Clueless, while Miss Delavigne’s New Zealand origins even brought back happy memories of Peter Jackson’s terrifying Heavenly Creatures. Flic and Minna’s friendship is based on a private language of their own, and you will have to acclimatise yourself to the stylised density of gags and zingers in the dialogue, which is worthy of Victoria Wood. When this secret world is contaminated by disloyal new alliances, it is very painful, especially for the person who feels left behind.

The movie leaves it up to us to decide if everything Flic and Minna do is just a diversion from the real thing: namely, their obvious feelings for each other. Or is it that their intense intimacy is immature and inauthentic, interesting only in that it is poignantly fated to evaporate when real grownup subjects are in play? Students of girl-power movies might sense another echo in the casting of Alice Englert; she starred with Elle Fanning in Sally Potter’s excellent Ginger & Rosa, which had a very similar dynamic. Extra Geography is an extra treat in the movie world’s school timetable.

title: What Sets High-Performing Pell Colleges Apart?
summary:
What Sets High-Performing Pell Colleges Apart?
Joshua.Bay Thu, 10/01/2026 - 03:00 AM

New research identifies 149 institutions with strong outcomes for Pell recipients—and suggests their success can’t be easily explained by resources, selectivity or student demographics.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Higher education has long been viewed as an avenue to economic mobility, but lower-income students continue to face disparities in college access and degree completion. Those gaps have persisted even as college enrollment has expanded, raising questions about which institutions are most successful at supporting lower-income students through graduation and into the workforce.

New research from the University of Wisconsin at Madison, published in AERA Open, identifies colleges and universities where Pell Grant recipients enroll and graduate at relatively high rates, face small completion gaps compared to their higher-income peers, and see strong earnings after college.

Drawing primarily on federal data from 1,462 four-year institutions from 2015–16 through 2019–20, researchers evaluated colleges across three dimensions: access for Pell recipients, degree completion and postgraduation earnings. They also examined whether institutions graduated Pell recipients at higher rates than expected based on their student populations, resources and other characteristics.

The researchers identified 149 high-performing Pell institutions that met their criteria. At those colleges, Pell recipients had an average graduation rate of 76.5 percent, compared with a 50 percent median across the broader sample. The average graduation gap between Pell and non-Pell students was 3.8 percentage points, compared with 13 points across the sample.

Taylor Odle, assistant professor at UW Madison and co-author of the study, said the institutions identified as high performing represent a wide range of colleges and universities, challenging assumptions about where strong outcomes for lower-income students are possible.

“Good work is being done across the higher education sector,” Odle said. “What we want to do is show that there is data out there that complicates some of the stories that we’ve always had in our minds, but that data can be used to make very high-stakes decisions in support of these lower-income students.”

Patterns of success: The list includes highly selective private institutions such as Harvard University, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Stanford University; public flagships including the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan and the University of Wisconsin at Madison; and liberal arts colleges such as Amherst College, Swarthmore College and Williams College.

The list also includes religiously affiliated institutions and colleges in urban, suburban and rural communities. Nearly all of the high-performing Pell institutions are public or private nonprofit colleges and universities, with three private for-profit institutions also making the list: Chamberlain University, DigiPen Institute of Technology and West Coast University.

“There’s this narrative in the policy space that student success can only be achieved at a certain subset of institutions that are heavily resourced or that are highly selective,” Odle said.

“We have public institutions, private institutions, rural, urban, highly selective and generally much broader access,” he added. “Institutions are showing that they can achieve not only high outcomes but equitable outcomes.”

Despite their strong outcomes for Pell recipients, high-performing Pell institutions did not necessarily enroll especially large populations of lower-income students. About one-quarter of students at the 149 institutions received a Pell Grant, compared with 38 percent across the broader sample.

Odle said higher education policy has historically placed significant emphasis on expanding college access, but increasing enrollment among lower-income students does not necessarily translate into higher completion rates.

“The strategies that we employ to get more students in the door and lower those involvement barriers are not the same strategies we need to use to help them through completion,” Odle said. “There are many institutions that you could look at nationally that enroll a ton of Pell recipients, but their Pell graduation rates are substantially lower, and I don’t think that’s an outcome that anybody would be particularly excited about.

“I’m glad that our policy conversations have moved to the space of ‘It’s not good enough to just get more folks from low-income backgrounds in the door. We need to be sure that they also have an equal chance of completing that degree and are having similar earnings to their non-Pell peers,’” he added.

Researchers also found that traditional measures of institutional quality, resources and student demographics did not fully explain why some colleges performed particularly well for Pell recipients. Factors such as student services spending, financial aid, admissions rates and the racial and socioeconomic makeup of the student body had limited ability to predict which institutions would qualify as high-performing Pell.

“Those predictors actually don’t do a really good job of explaining why an institution appears to be on this list,” Odle said. “There’s something else going on, and we need more political investment, we need more research and we need more private partnerships to find out what that secret sauce is.”

Sky Duke, a doctoral student at Madison and co-author of the report, said the findings suggest researchers may need to look beyond individual programs or interventions to understand how an institution’s broader environment contributes to Pell student success.

“It’s not necessarily going to be just one intervention that’s happening in isolation in that institution, but rather a combination,” Duke said. “That environmental piece is really worth investigating further.”

Beyond access: Duke said the study offers a broader way of thinking about socioeconomic equity in higher education by considering whether colleges provide access to low-income students, support them through degree completion and position them for economic mobility after graduation.

“It’s not necessarily an issue with the students,” she said. “But simply that, given an appropriate environment that can uplift them and support them through completion … these things are possible.”

Duke said identifying the 149 institutions is a starting point for understanding what they are doing differently and whether those approaches could work elsewhere.

“Now that we have the data, [we can] start following up and investigating to see how these things can expand to different institutions that are looking to improve success rates,” she said.

Odle said the findings are particularly relevant in the current political environment, where “we can’t not ask about completion and labor-market outcomes for these colleges.”

“It relates to what we hope people do with this work,” he said. “It’s not just getting low-income students in the door. It’s also graduating them at high rates and making sure that they have positive and relatively strong labor-market earnings when they leave.”

title: Historic $3B Gift to Fund New Campus for Carnegie Mellon
summary:
Historic $3B Gift to Fund New Campus for Carnegie Mellon
Susan H. Greenberg Thu, 10/01/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Susan H. Greenberg
full_text:
Carnegie Mellon University has received a historic $3 billion donation from Citadel founder and CEO Ken Griffin, the largest individual gift ever given to a higher ed institution.

Two-thirds of the funds will be used to launch a new campus, CMU Miami, which will focus on advancing research and discovery to solve society’s greatest challenges in areas such as human health, national security and climate resilience. The campus will also support innovation in teaching and hands-on learning.

Construction on the Miami campus is expected to begin in 2027, with the first students enrolling in 2028; eventually CMU Miami will house more than 3,500 undergraduate, master’s and Ph.D. students, nearly 300 faculty, and over 600 staff members.

“Since its founding, Carnegie Mellon has fostered remarkable talent, pioneered scientific breakthroughs, and expanded the frontiers of research—shaping global leaders and innovators,” Griffin said in a statement. “The opportunity to bring Carnegie Mellon to Miami places our city at the heart of humanistic and scientific advancement and amplifies the University’s international reach and impact. It is a tremendous privilege to be part of this historic moment.”

The remaining $1 billion of his gift will go toward CMU’s Pittsburgh campus, where it will be split evenly between funding the university’s rotating slate of top priorities and supporting the computer science school, which will now be known as the Kenneth C. Griffin School of Computer Science.

“We are deeply grateful to Ken Griffin for his extraordinary vision, partnership and belief in what Carnegie Mellon can achieve,” said CMU President Farnam Jahanian. “Throughout our history, CMU has anticipated moments of profound technological change and responded with new ways of thinking and solving problems … Together, we have an opportunity to extend the very qualities that have long distinguished Carnegie Mellon—our agility, creativity, interdisciplinary culture and relentless focus on impact—to build a new model for higher education that meets the urgency of this moment.”

title: College Affordability’s Hidden Variable
summary:
College Affordability’s Hidden Variable
quintina.barne… Thu, 10/01/2026 - 03:00 AM

Credit evaluation in admissions supports affordability.

Byline(s)
Jesse Boeding
full_text:
A few days after dropping off her son, Alex, for his first year of college, my friend shared move-in photos with the bittersweet pride of a parent watching a child begin a new chapter. However, since that drop-off, however, more bitter than sweet has overtaken the family. Alex had met with his academic adviser and learned that his AP and dual-enrollment credits would not count toward his program.

Only after arriving at college did he discover that, rather than graduating a semester early, he would instead require a full extra semester of school. Alex still had time to withdraw from his classes and receive a full refund, but after moving to campus and beginning college life, that option had become far more difficult, both practically and emotionally.

Alex isn’t alone. Hundreds of other students discover only after arriving at college that effort they expended in high school to reduce the cost of higher education will not play out as they expected.

This is why credit evaluation belongs in the admissions cycle, not the enrollment cycle. If learners are to make informed decisions about affordability, they must know how their prior learning will apply to a degree and how those decisions will affect their entire bottom line—including time and expense.

Affordability is a headline for a reason. Higher education sticker prices can be difficult for families to comprehend, even when they do not reflect what students will actually pay. According to preliminary estimates from the National Association of College and University Business Officers, private nonprofit colleges’ average tuition discount rate for first-time, full-time undergraduates reached 57.1 percent in 2025–26—the highest in the study’s history. That doesn’t mean $25,800 is affordable, but it is certainly less than $60,000.

To address concerns about affordability, higher education has shifted toward mapping clearer paths from education to employment. The logic is understandable: Better information about in-demand careers, required credentials and expected salaries can help learners assess whether an educational investment is worthwhile.

Yet careers rarely unfold as neatly as pathway maps suggest. Economic cycles, technological change, geography, personality, relationships and luck all shape individual outcomes. Just two years ago, computer science was widely promoted as one of the safest routes to stable, well-paying work; artificial intelligence has downgraded that outlook. Learners should understand the employment prospects they may face after graduation, but career pathways cannot predict how an individual career or an entire field will change, and presenting career pathways as predictable risks disappointing learners and inviting criticism of institutions.

We cannot guarantee the future, but we can do a much better job of telling learners what it will cost them to get a degree at a specific institution. Changing the way we talk about college affordability requires that we look beyond providing a generalized estimate. Millions have been invested in helping learners understand and reduce the cost of higher education, but seeking a degree is not like buying a car and reading the price on the window sticker. A prospective student is purchasing the opportunity to learn over a set period of time, but they aren’t told what that time might be for them. Institutions own the decision that makes that number much clearer.

The net price calculator was supposed to be an important part of that clarifying process, helping learners to look beyond the tuition and estimate what college would really cost. But it fails, because the number it produces is incomplete. The calculator may show learners what a year of college will cost, but it can’t tell them how many years or semesters they will need to buy. It does not show how the overall cost is impacted when AP credits are rejected, or dual-enrollment coursework does not apply, or if transfer, military or prior learning credits disappear during an institution’s evaluation process.

Colleges and learners both tend to concentrate on the financial side of the affordability equation: tuition, scholarships, grants, loans and room and board. We have, however, neglected to invest that attention in the variable that can dramatically affect the total price: time.

Time highlights more than the tuition a learner pays; it homes in on how many rounds of fees, housing, food and other costs a learner accrues. It determines how long students wait before entering the full-time workforce. For learners already working, it can determine how long they must balance employment, family responsibilities and their schooling.

Prior learning has the potential to reduce that time and therefore the actual cost of completing a degree. Yet most institutions wait until orientation or add/drop to provide students clear credit evaluations. A website may display an equivalency chart or direct learners to “see your department for information.” Like Alex, a learner may not receive a definite answer until after they start classes.

Well before that, however, learners receive detailed financial aid offers, showing tuition, scholarships, grants, loans, expected family contributions, room and board estimates, and lists of fees. Missing is the number that could materially change their decision: How much of the learning that you have already completed will count toward this degree?

Imagine if an admission offer did not simply say, “We are awarding you a $12,000 scholarship.” Imagine that it also said, “We have evaluated the [AP, IB, dual-enrollment and other eligible learning] you submitted. In total, [#] credits will apply to your degree. Based on your program and course sequence, that will reduce your anticipated completion time by [#] semester, reducing your degree’s cost by $XX.”

That second offer provides the learner something much closer to a complete picture of the price of their education.

It’s a classic sales strategy, to provide clarifying information after the buyer has emotionally committed. Alex’s AP credits did not suddenly become less valuable when he met with his adviser. His school just waited until that point to tell him what they were worth there.

Let me be clear: I am not saying that all credits must be accepted. There are legitimate reasons some credits should not apply. The learning may not be equivalent, it may not meet the requirements of a specific program or it may not represent a college-level learning experience.

Institutions should absolutely protect academic standards, and faculty should determine whether learning meets the expectations of a course or credential in their department. When colleges believe certain dual-enrollment courses do not constitute college-level learning, they should clearly explain that, and any major-specific limitations, to the schools and learners who are told those courses will earn college credit.

Earlier evaluation may require additional faculty and staff time or more thorough, efficient processes. Even so, helping learners understand the actual time and cost required to earn a degree is integral to the admissions process, rather than a minor detail that can be handled later if affordability is mission-critical.

Institutions may worry that awarding credit for prior learning means losing tuition revenue. Yet, over more than a decade, research from the Council for Adult and Experiential Learning has shown that adult learners awarded credit for prior learning are more likely to complete a credential—two and a half times as likely in a 2010 study and 17 percent more likely in a 2020 study with WICHE that controlled for other factors. CAEL survey data also suggest that the availability of such credit shapes where and whether adults choose to enroll.

Colleges spend enormous sums discounting tuition and offering scholarships to attract learners, while overlooking the time asset they could be including in admissions offers. Awarding a learner 15 credits for prior learning may appear to mean forfeiting 15 credits of tuition revenue. However, the question may become whether the college would prefer to have that learner enroll for seven semesters or lose them entirely because another institution offered a clearer, more affordable or shorter route to completion.

We don’t need career predictions to give learners information we already know: What will the institution accept of the learning they’ve already completed? What will apply to their degree? How much time in school will that save them and how will that saved time affect their actual cost? To demonstrate we are truly committed to affordability, we must reveal the cost of time.

If colleges really believe that higher education should be more affordable, affordability cannot be defined by career projections or tuition discounts. It must also include how many credits, and therefore time, institutions are awarding. For learners (and families) who are making one of the largest financial decisions of their lives, time has a price.

title: College Leaders Prepare to Administer Workforce Pell as ED Approves Programs
summary:
College Leaders Prepare to Administer Workforce Pell as ED Approves Programs
Olivia.sanchez Thu, 10/01/2026 - 03:00 AM

Institutions have to ensure that their financial aid officers and software systems are ready to administer aid for short-term programs and that students know the opportunity exists.

Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
The long-awaited debut of Workforce Pell has finally arrived. Later this month, Ivy Tech Community College in Indiana will begin doling out federal financial aid dollars to eligible students in an eight-week clinical medical assistant program. When they do, Ivy Tech will become one of the first colleges in the nation to accept Pell Grants as payment for certain short-term career-oriented programs.

After years of policy debate, Congress in summer 2025 passed legislation that allows federal Pell dollars—financial aid for low-income students—to be used on programs between eight and 15 weeks long rather than a full year or longer. That triggered a yearlong sprint for federal and state leaders to figure out how to work together to determine which programs would qualify for approval by state governments and the U.S. Education Department. The rollout has been slow so far; since the policy took effect on July 1, ED has approved 21 programs across six states, including Florida, Indiana, Iowa, Nebraska, North Carolina, Texas.

But for colleges, the work doesn’t stop when a program is approved. College leaders need to make sure that their financial aid officers and their software systems are equipped to process federal grants for short-term programs. They also must communicate the new funding opportunity to prospective students and encourage them to fill out the Free Application for Federal Student Aid—something students haven’t historically needed to do when enrolling in short-term, career-oriented programs.

“This is a pretty substantial policy change and policy implementation ask of states and institutions and even ED,” said Iris Palmer, director of the community college initiative at New America, a left-leaning think tank. Now, as programs are being approved, “this is going to take a huge lift from [college] financial aid offices.”

Colby Shank, vice president of financial aid and student accounts at Ivy Tech, said the college submitted an application for its certified medical assistant program on July 7 and was approved on Aug. 19.

“We were very excited, but then we also recognized that that’s just kind of the beginning,” Shank said. There were “a lot of questions on how we take approval to implementation.”

When Ivy Tech begins accepting Pell Grants for the program in late October, the grants will fund up to a dozen students on just one of the community college system’s 19 campuses. Shank said he expects two other campuses to accept Workforce Pell for the certified medical assistant program soon.

“It’s rewarding to be able to offer a new avenue for financial aid when, on the short-term-program side, the options have historically been fairly limited,” Shank said. “But right now, we expect it will be a lot of manual work.”

Shank explained that Ivy Tech’s software system isn’t set up to process financial aid for short-term programs, which will require financial aid officers to manually identify eligible students, calculate their Workforce Pell award based on their need and the length of their program, and personally disburse the funds to students.

“We’re starting to explore what it will take with our software systems to scale this, which is what we want to see happen,” Shank said. “But in the meantime, to get us off the ground, we plan on doing quite a bit of this work manually just so that we can serve students as quickly as possible.”

Iowa Central Community College, whose 14-week emergency medical technician program was the first in the country to be approved for Workforce Pell, hasn’t faced the same financial aid system challenges as Ivy Tech because it offers a Pell-eligible commercial driver’s license program, said Stacy Mentzer, the college’s vice president of instruction. Their system was already able to calculate financial aid based on clock hours rather than credit hours, so it was easier to make the adjustments necessary to offer Workforce Pell, she added.

The college is currently recruiting students for its next cycle and encouraging them to fill out the FAFSA to see if they’re eligible for Workforce Pell; it will begin offering the course when enough students have enrolled, Mentzer said.

Some colleges are more focused on making students aware of the new program.

Janet N. Spriggs, president of Forsyth Technical Community College in North Carolina, said she is trying to figure out how to inform as many students as possible about the new funding option for the six programs Forsyth has had approved: welding, certified nursing assistant (levels one and two), fire academy, emergency medical technician, and electrical line worker. She said Forsyth Tech plans to enroll students with Workforce Pell starting in January.

“It is another pathway forward for our students to be able to get the skills that they need for careers that are going to give them family-sustaining and family-thriving wages,” Spriggs said. “The most important part is not letting this wonderful opportunity be a secret.”

Spriggs said Forsyth is working with high school career coaches, employers and community organizations to spread the word about Workforce Pell. Although she knows it won’t help every student or support training for every career pathway, “for those that it will, it’s going to have a huge impact,” Spriggs said.

title: UK TNE students near 700k as overseas provision overtakes onshore international enrolment
summary:
UK universities are now educating more students overseas through transnational education (TNE) than they are hosting international students onshore.

The post UK TNE students near 700k as overseas provision overtakes onshore international enrolment appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
According to new data from Universities UK International (UUKi), the number of students studying for UK higher education qualifications through TNE reached 699,660 in 2024–25, up 7% year-on-year and 36.6% over five years.

The figure is now higher than the 681,430 international students studying in the UK, highlighting the growing scale of UK universities’ overseas provision.

The findings come from the latest edition of UUKi’s ‘The scale of UK higher education transnational education’, published as the sector continues to grapple with changes in international student mobility and demand for UK degrees.

In total, 183 UK higher education providers delivered TNE across 229 countries and territories during 2024–25.

“With TNE playing a vital role in widening global access to UK degrees, this report shows how our universities are at the forefront of this profound shift,” said Jamie Arrowsmith, director of UUKi.

“As the landscape continues to evolve, we’re committed to supporting our members in developing their provision, ensuring that growth in TNE remains strategic, sustainable, and rooted in partnership and mutual benefit.”

As the landscape continues to evolve, we’re committed to supporting our members in developing their provision, ensuring that growth in TNE remains strategic, sustainable, and rooted in partnership and mutual benefit

Jamie Arrowsmith, UUKi

Asia remained the largest host region, accounting for 51% of all UK TNE students in 2024–25.

South Asia recorded particularly rapid growth, with 124,500 students, a 76.9% increase compared with 2020–21. East Asia hosted a further 118,270 students, up 35.6% over the same period, while Southeast Asia hosted 99,795, an increase of 14.3%.

Central and Western Asia accounted for a further 13,885 students, representing growth of 53.2% over five years.

Europe remained the second-largest host region despite a decline in student numbers, accounting for 16.3% of UK TNE students. It was followed by the Middle East, with 14.8%, and Africa, with 12.5%.

North America accounted for 4.4% of UK TNE students, while South America and Australasia represented 0.7% and 0.4% respectively.

All major forms of UK TNE provision have grown since 2020–21, although the pace of growth has varied.

Partnership provision recorded the largest increase, with student numbers rising 51.4% over five years. Overseas campus provision grew by 30.3%, while distance learning increased by 6.8%.

Fewer than 3% of students worldwide are internationally mobile, according to UUKi, meaning the majority of students seeking higher education continue to study in their home countries.

The organisation said TNE therefore provides a route for UK universities to meet international demand without requiring students to relocate.

Earlier this year, the UK government revealed its refreshed international education strategy, including an ambitious aim to grow education exports to £40 billion per year by 2030, citing TNE as a core pillar of growth.

The UUKi report has been released alongside a new international higher education dashboard from the Higher Education Statistics Agency (HESA), part of Jisc.

The interactive tool brings together data on international students studying at UK institutions and TNE students studying overseas, with data available from 2012–13.

Users can compare international student numbers and TNE provision by higher education provider and country of origin.

title: Teaching Cyber Threats Differently: An AI-Powered Gamified Approach
summary:
While many academics are still locked in debate about whether to allow artificial intelligence in the classroom — fearing academic dishonesty, over-reliance, or loss of rigor — I made a deliberate choice to do the opposite. I brought AI in, put it at the center of the assessment, and asked my students to challenge it.  […]

The post Teaching Cyber Threats Differently: An AI-Powered Gamified Approach appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
While many academics are still locked in debate about whether to allow artificial intelligence in the classroom — fearing academic dishonesty, over-reliance, or loss of rigor — I made a deliberate choice to do the opposite. I brought AI in, put it at the center of the assessment, and asked my students to challenge it.

That decision was not taken lightly. The dilemma is real: AI tools can write essays, solve problems, and generate code with startling fluency. For many educators, this feels like a threat to the integrity of learning. But in a cybersecurity classroom, I saw a different possibility. What if AI were not the shortcut we feared, but the instrument through which students developed sharper, more critical thinking?

At Majan University College, I ventured where many colleagues hesitated — and the results reshaped how I teach cyber threats entirely.

The Dilemma Most Academics Face

The debate around AI in higher education is genuine and ongoing. Concerns about academic integrity are legitimate. When a student can paste an assignment question into ChatGPT and receive a polished response in seconds, the traditional essay or report begins to feel obsolete as an assessment instrument. Many institutions have responded with blanket bans or AI-detection policies.

But in a field like cybersecurity — where AI tools are already embedded in professional practice — banning them from the classroom risks producing graduates who are technically unprepared for the workplace. The question I kept returning to was not whether to allow AI, but how to design learning around it so that critical thinking remained non-negotiable.

“The question was not whether to allow AI, but how to design learning around it so that critical thinking remained non-negotiable.”

The Problem with Traditional Cybersecurity Instruction

Cybersecurity changes faster than most curricula can keep up with. Threat actors adapt weekly, new vulnerabilities emerge daily, and students are expected to master concepts ranging from network intrusion to social engineering — often in a single module. Lecture-based instruction struggles to keep pace.

In my own classroom, I noticed a recurring pattern: students could recite definitions of common vulnerabilities but froze when asked to identify them in a live network scenario. The knowledge was there — the application was not. I needed a method that built not just understanding, but instinct.

Step 1: Real Tools, Real Vulnerabilities

The first shift was putting industry-grade tools directly in students’ hands. Through a free licence from Tenable, students registered for and used Nessus Essentials — the same vulnerability scanner used by professional penetration testers — to scan their own lab environments and identify real weaknesses.

This was not a simulation. Students discovered actual vulnerabilities in their own machines: open ports, misconfigured services, outdated software with known exploits. The moment a student sees Nessus flag a critical-severity bind shell backdoor on their own system, the abstract becomes concrete. Cybersecurity stops being a theory module and starts feeling like a professional responsibility.

Figure 1 — Topic 7: Network Traffic Monitoring on MOVE (Majan E-Learning), showing Nessus Essentials registration, microlearning certificate upload, and the AI tools forum activity.

Step 2: Compare Three AI Tools, Then Decide

Once students identified a vulnerability, the next task was not to fix it immediately. Instead, they were asked to consult three AI tools of their choice — such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Claude AI — and compare the remediation approaches each one suggested. They then had to evaluate which solution was most technically sound, justify their choice, and document their reasoning in a forum post.

This comparative exercise produced some of the richest academic discussion I have seen in a computing module. Students quickly discovered that different AI tools gave meaningfully different answers — not just in wording, but in technical depth, persistence, and correctness. One student’s analysis of a critical bind shell backdoor (CVE-linked, severity 10.0) illustrated this perfectly.

Figure 2 — A student’s submitted report comparing Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini remediation approaches for a critical bind shell backdoor vulnerability discovered using Nessus Essentials.

As the student’s report showed, Claude’s approach — disabling the ingreslock entry in /etc/inetd.conf and de-registering the xinetd super-server — permanently removed the vulnerability at its source and survived reboots. ChatGPT’s suggestion to kill the process was effective in the moment but non-persistent. Gemini’s firewall rule blocked external access but left the backdoor process running locally. The student chose Claude’s method because it satisfied NIST SP 800-53 SI-2 requirements.

This kind of critical AI literacy — knowing not just how to use AI tools but how to evaluate and challenge their outputs — is precisely what the cybersecurity industry needs from the next generation of practitioners.

“Students discovered that different AI tools gave meaningfully different answers — not just in wording, but in technical depth, persistence, and correctness.”

Step 3: Microlearning Before Every Lab

Supporting both the Nessus work and the AI comparison tasks was a restructured content delivery model. Rather than front-loading a two-hour lecture, I broke module content into focused microlearning units of five to ten minutes each — delivered on MOVE, Majan’s e-learning platform, before each lab session.

Each unit was deliberately brief and focused, ensuring students arrived at labs already familiar with the core concept — meaning lab time could be spent entirely on application rather than explanation. A microlearning certificate upload task on MOVE reinforced completion and accountability without adding administrative burden.

At Majan University College, where many students balance studies with work and family responsibilities, the flexibility of microlearning also reduced cognitive overload. Bite-sized content reviewable on a phone during a commute proved far more accessible than dense lecture recordings.

What the Results Showed

After one full semester using this combined approach, the outcomes were encouraging. Student performance on practical assessments — particularly those requiring live vulnerability identification and remediation — improved noticeably compared to previous cohorts. Student feedback consistently highlighted increased confidence in applying tools independently, and the forum posts demonstrated a level of critical analytical writing that prior cohorts had rarely produced.

Several students who had previously struggled with abstract networking concepts were among the most engaged contributors to the AI comparison discussions. The practical, tool-driven format appeared to level the playing field in ways that traditional assessment had not.

Three Takeaways for Fellow Educators

1. Start with Nessus Essentials. Tenable offers free licences for students and educators. Having students scan their own machines creates an immediate, personal connection to the vulnerability concepts you are teaching.

2. Make AI comparison the assessment, not AI use. Asking students to compare three AI tools’ outputs builds critical thinking and AI literacy simultaneously — far more valuable than letting them use a single tool uncritically.

3. Keep microlearning units under ten minutes and single-topic. Pair each unit with a concrete lab task so the knowledge is applied within the same session it is introduced.

Cybersecurity education is no longer just about teaching student’s what threats exist. It is about equipping them to think like defenders in a world where the threats change faster than the textbooks — and where AI tools are both an asset and a variable that must itself be critically evaluated. What began as an experiment at Majan University College has become the foundation of how I approach every cybersecurity module I teach.

This is an abridged version of the full peer-reviewed article: A Pedagogical Framework for Embedding Microlearning, Gamification, and Industry Credentials in Undergraduate Cybersecurity Education — Ramalingam Dharmalingam, Majan University College, Muscat, Sultanate of Oman.

title: Higher Ed’s Path to Advanced Cybersecurity Maturity
summary:
Higher education institutions face increasing pressure to strengthen cybersecurity while maintaining agility and cost-efficiency. IT leaders must move beyond reactive defense and toward operationalized maturity — creating systems that are resilient, scalable and audit-ready.
Using guidance from the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Cybersecurity Framework and FINRA’s cybersecurity practices, enterprise-grade security principles can be adapted for use by security leaders for colleges and universities.
This includes advanced zero-trust implementation and…
full_text:
By adopting these approaches, higher education IT leaders can transform security from a cost center into a growth enabler — achieving high-level protection and compliance without sacrificing innovation or speed.

Advanced Zero-Trust Implementation for Higher Education

Aaron Bugal, field CISO for Sophos, explains that zero trust is a journey, not necessarily a specific technology choice or stack. Rather, it is a blend of process, people and technology.

He says that identity has become the new security perimeter, requiring phishing-resistant, auditable, multifactor authentication to verify users and devices continuously.

Network segmentation limits the blast radius of breaches, while modern firewalls combining software-defined WAN, VPN and zero-trust capabilities simplify secure access. Continuous verification and automation enhance visibility and reduce manual workload, maintaining “transient trust” that adapts in real time.

“Around-the-clock detection and response are essential, making 24/7 monitoring and early alert investigation critical,” Bugal says. He adds that leveraging external expertise and automation can strengthen defenses and free teams to focus on strategic risk reduction.

READ MORE: Higher ed institutions are adopting zero-trust strategies.

WatchGuard field CTO Adam Winston says that when integrating EDR with SIEM and SOAR platforms, the goal should be to measure efficiency in the security operations center.

This can be achieved by setting up metrics such as mean time to respond or contain and running regular simulations to identify areas for improvement — without the pressure of real-world scenarios. “Organizations should start by ensuring that their EDR telemetry feeds directly into the SIEM to provide centralized visibility,” Winston says.

Teams can then use breach and attack simulation tools to routinely test the detection of new threats.

Winston adds that it’s important to tune SOAR playbooks based on test results to improve automated containment and facilitate case enrichment. “That way, teams can validate that the data is normalized and consistent across EDR, SIEM and SOAR for accurate correlation,” he says.

Continuous Exposure Management Strategies

Michelle Abraham, research vice president at IDC, says visibility into all of an organization’s assets is the foundation of exposure management. “The asset data should be aggregated and managed holistically, so all risks can be managed as one instead of in silos,” she explains.

DISCOVER: Continuous threat exposure management helps higher ed prioritize risk.

Once the exposures and their associated assets are prioritized based on their importance to the organization, remediation or mitigation efforts remove or block exposures from being exploited by attackers.

“Since exposures are found faster than ever, organizations need to move more quickly to fix issues as well,” Abraham notes.

Dana Simberkoff, chief risk, privacy and information security officer at AvePoint, says identity threat detection and response (ITDR) naturally complements zero-trust architectures by ensuring even verified, authenticated users are behaving within expected parameters.

“Your users — humans — are always going to be your weakest link,” Simberkoff says. “By focusing not only on identity but also content and context, you can help to make sure that human error does not lead to catastrophic consequences.”

Winston adds that a mature ITDR solution should respond to account creation and removal and continuously detect and respond to identity misuse across sessions, devices and behaviors.

title: Pre-arrival insight helps institutions provide earlier and more targeted student support
summary: The post Pre-arrival insight helps institutions provide earlier and more targeted student support appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
New case studies show how HE institutions are using insight gathered before students begin their studies to strengthen transition activity, coordinate services and offer support sooner.

Higher education institutions taking part in the Pre-arrival Academic Questionnaire (PAQ) are already using early insight to make practical changes. Findings from the first wave of results have helped staff identify mental health, disability, study and financial support needs, inform induction and Welcome Week planning, develop student resources and improve coordination between academic teams and professional services.

The PAQ captures students’ confidence, concerns and expectations before they enter higher education, giving providers evidence to support more informed and responsive transition planning. The first wave of the national pilot was delivered in 2025 by Advance HE, the University of East London and Jisc, with responses from incoming undergraduates at 15 higher education institutions in England.

How institutions are putting the insight into practice

The initial findings show why pre-arrival insight matters. They point to differences in students’ confidence and preparedness, expectations of higher education, digital experience, financial pressures and wellbeing concerns before study begins.

A series of new case studies published by Advance HE show how institutions are turning that evidence into earlier, more inclusive and better-coordinated support, responding to students’ circumstances and expectations before pressures emerge.

Norland University of Early Childhood

For Norland, the PAQ reinforced the value of existing support while providing fresh evidence about what incoming students need. Sharing the findings with academic governance, senior leaders and support teams has encouraged a more joined-up approach to student feedback and future survey delivery, with early insight being used to strengthen wellbeing and student success.

SOAS

At SOAS, the impact is still developing, but the first findings are already helping to shape Welcome Week, transition support and planning for the 2026 intake. The data has revealed differences between international and UK postgraduate students, deepened understanding of their expectations and needs, and highlighted opportunities to strengthen academic engagement and future delivery of the questionnaire.

Southampton Solent University

Southampton Solent University used the PAQ to build a substantial evidence base for strategic discussion and practical planning across governance, academic departments and professional services. The findings are shaping thinking about library workshops, study support and how placement opportunities are communicated, while giving staff a clearer view of students’ motivations, expectations, financial pressures, sense of belonging and support needs. The pilot also showed how earlier engagement and closer integration of the findings could strengthen future decision-making.

UCEN Manchester

At UCEN Manchester, the PAQ helped staff identify mental health, disability, study and financial support needs at an earlier stage, enabling tutors and specialist teams to offer targeted help before concerns escalated. Bringing the findings into personal tutorials also strengthened staff engagement with student insight and supported a more coordinated approach to surveys and feedback.

University of Portsmouth

The University of Portsmouth used the PAQ to identify students who might benefit from early help with employment or disability-related support. Sharing the findings across leadership, faculties and professional services encouraged a coordinated response, while communicating headline results to students helped close the feedback loop and inform future induction and support activity.

University of Worcester

At the University of Worcester, the PAQ provided a clear route from student reflection to institutional action. Strong engagement during induction informed a student support booklet, governance discussions and practical developments including plans for a commuter lounge. It also brought academic and professional service teams together around a shared understanding of the incoming student experience.

Next steps

The second wave of the PAQ national pilot is now underway, involving 22 institutions across England, Scotland and Wales and covering undergraduate and postgraduate taught programmes.

Findings from the second wave will be published in early 2027, providing further evidence of how pre-arrival insight can support transition planning and earlier intervention. The findings and wider learning from participating institutions will also inform discussions at a sector conference on 22 April 2027.

title: 6 of the Most Prestigious Online Master’s Degrees
summary: A Masters Degree can be a Key to a Great Career (Source: Depositphotos) A graduate degree can help you strategically develop the skills employers are looking for. It may also help you get a foot in the door of exciting work that pays more over the long term. We’ve hand-picked six online degrees to help […]
full_text:
A graduate degree can help you strategically develop the skills employers are looking for. It may also help you get a foot in the door of exciting work that pays more over the long term.

We’ve hand-picked six online degrees to help you decide if grad school is the right move for you.

They range from programs that help techies specialize in exciting fields to options for breaking into computing and degrees that teach you how to manage communications.

Whatever your career aspirations, one of these programs might be right up your alley. And since they’re all offered online, you can jump-start your career without giving up your job or moving across the country.

A few caveats first. This is not a formal ranking of programs.

Career tracks indicate careers that can be pursued with the skills you’d learn in these programs. They are not guarantees that you’ll be hired after graduation.

Salary information is in U.S. dollars, for U.S. careers, unless otherwise indicated. Medians are national, meaning they reflect people in these fields with various levels of experience. So don’t necessarily expect to earn the median upon graduation.

6

Stanford University: MS in Computer Science

Stanford’s MS in Computer Science is an online program that offers depth and breadth of knowledge to take your technical chops to the next level. It’s designed for software engineers and computer scientists who want to move beyond implementing others’ solutions to working on core technical issues.

Through the Honors Cooperative Program, you can keep working as you pursue a master’s in CS with a specialization in Systems, Artificial Intelligence, or Information Management and Analytics.1

These three tracks can be completed online, while others require some in-person participation. The program is open to U.S. residents only.1 Graduates may pursue careers in machine learning engineering, advanced software development, data infrastructure, and systems engineering.

Best for: This is a good option if you’re an app developer facing scaling problems and want to better understand and evaluate technology and reason about system design. The program may help you advance your career without changing employers. It’s a strong option for those who can draw a clear line from a specialization to future job responsibilities.

Why a master’s in computer science?

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reports that the median annual wage for software developers was $135,980 in May 2025.2 Plus, some employers prefer candidates with a master’s degree.2

5

Columbia University: MS in Computer Science

Columbia University offers an online master of science (MS) degree in computer science through its online platform, the Columbia Video Network.3 The curriculum prepares students to apply theoretical knowledge, as well as to use and contribute to new, experimental technologies.

Applicants are encouraged to have a background in computer science. However, candidates from other fields may be considered if they have the appropriate college-level computer science and math coursework.3

Students may specialize in topics like machine learning through Columbia’s online machine learning track, which prepares them for careers in intelligent software and predictive models.4

What you’ll be able to do with this degree

Computer science MS degree holders may pursue careers in fields such as machine learning engineering, software engineering, or research. Note that building software that meets a company’s needs is different from developing new and innovative technology. Careers that require more of the latter include computer and information research scientists, who study fundamental computing problems and develop solutions.

According to the BLS, this field typically requires a master’s degree for entry-level positions, though employers may prefer candidates with a doctorate.5 In May 2025, computer and information research scientists earned a median annual wage of $140,300.5

How to tell if a computer science MS is right for you

Review a few job postings in fields that interest you to see if this type of degree could help you reach your professional goals. Many tech careers require an understanding of algorithms and methods of computing. If many listings call for these skills, especially in areas like machine learning, a computer science master’s could be helpful.

While working through the program, use your classes to create projects that show you can apply what you’ve learned.

An MS can open doors, but employers generally want to see that you can apply your skills to real projects.

4

University of Pennsylvania: Master of Applied Science in Computer Science Online

The Master of Applied Science in Computer Science Online (MAS-CS Online), offered through the University of Pennsylvania, is one of our recommended online master’s degrees. It can help you learn the fundamentals of programming, computer science, computer systems, algorithms, and software design, then apply these skills to advance your career. MAS-CS Online will replace Penn’s MCIT Online program beginning in fall 2026.6

Can a CS-related online master’s get you hired as a programmer, software engineer, or in another technical role if you don’t already have a CS background? The short answer is that it can.

The longer answer is that it’ll take some legwork on your part. You’ll need to make sure you have the requisite technical chops and are prepared to ace any technical interviews.

Designed especially for career-changers, MAS-CS Online aims to help you combine your current knowledge in a field (health care, education, finance) with a passion and skill set for building software solutions or working on a team creating software products.6

Graduates of the predecessor MCIT program who landed a new job after completing it had an average salary of $141,696, Penn reports.6

With a MAS-CS Online degree, you may pursue a career as a software engineer or product engineer, or in an AI-focused or data-related role. Students can focus on areas of study including artificial intelligence, data science, cybersecurity, and engineering entrepreneurship.6

3

Johns Hopkins University: MS in Artificial Intelligence

The Johns Hopkins University (JHU) master’s degree in Artificial Intelligence can teach you how to design intelligent systems that help businesses and other organizations improve their processes and operations.7

The fully online degree is offered through the university’s Engineering for Professionals program. It also draws on input from JHU’s Applied Physics Laboratory to build the curriculum. Topics include machine learning, natural language processing (NLP), image processing, and robotics.7

After earning your degree, you may be prepared for roles like AI engineer, machine learning engineer, data scientist, software developer integrating AI into products, computer research scientist, and more.

Data scientists earned a median annual wage of $120,230 in May 2025, and employers may prefer or require them to have a master’s or doctoral degree.8

Is this program right for me?

Ask yourself if you’re excited to learn how AI works under the hood. If you’re interested in understanding and designing AI technologies like text-processing and document-analysis tools (NLP), computer-vision applications (image processing), or intelligent, adaptive, or self-organizing systems for classification, prediction, or decision-making (machine learning), this could be the degree for you.

If you like programming and solving problems with mathematics, and would love to take ownership of AI projects from conception and design to modeling and testing, consider this program.

Think about whether you want to spend your workdays solving AI-related technical and engineering problems, rather than tinkering with the latest AI-powered tools or responding to AI-related headlines. If you’re looking to learn about AI in depth, JHU’s program could be a good fit.

2

Imperial College London: MSc in Machine Learning and Data Science

Machine learning and data science are fast-growing fields. If you’re interested in a career in data science and have a solid quantitative background, Imperial College London offers an MSc in Machine Learning and Data Science entirely online.9

It’s a two-year, part-time degree that focuses on the mathematically intensive parts of data science, like probability and statistical methods, deep learning, and reinforcement learning. The degree culminates in an extensive research project applying these skills to a machine learning problem, like detecting unusual financial transactions or forecasting future demand. The program is housed in Imperial’s Department of Mathematics.9

Why math?

It’s important to know how to write the code that trains and implements a model. But it’s even more important to know what happens if customer behavior changes, or if you’re shown a whole new kind of data and your model doesn’t perform well.

Knowing how reliable your model is, and how far you can push its predictions, is crucial if these models are going to inform important business decisions.

After completing this degree, graduates may go on to become data scientists or machine learning engineers, or find jobs in applied research.

According to the BLS, the median annual wage for U.S. data scientists was $120,230 in May 2025, with the highest-paid 10 percent earning over $199,130.8 Keep in mind, though, that this isn’t necessarily what you can expect to make as an Imperial grad.

1

University of Southern California: Master of Communication Management

USC Annenberg offers a Master of Communication Management program that can be taken entirely online.10 It may be a good option if you’re looking to advance into a management or leadership role in strategic communications.

Students can apply their writing, speaking, and relationship-building abilities to bigger-picture skills like audience analysis, media strategy, and research. Along the way, they learn how to advise executives, manage messaging and media campaigns, and lead a team.

The goal of the program is to educate the next generation of leaders who can connect messaging and media directly to business decisions. Students learn how to develop messages based on a thorough understanding of target audiences, select the most effective channels, work with other departments to achieve messaging goals, and measure the success of their work. Specializations are available in marketing communication; media, entertainment, and creator industries; and strategic and organizational communication.10

Public relations managers earned a median annual wage of $146,910 in May 2025, per the BLS,11 while marketing managers earned a median of $166,790.12

But many of these positions require experience in a related occupation.11, 12 So the median wages for management positions are best seen as a long-term career goal.

Consider what roles you’re hoping to achieve and weigh that against the cost of the degree.

Think about what experience you already have and which skills from a master’s degree could fill any gaps.

title: Digitale Souveränität: Die definitive Definition
summary:
Wie werden wir digital souverän, und was heißt das – eigentlich klar so weit, oder? Nein, für die meisten ist es das noch nicht. Während die einen schon eine feste Definition in ihren Zielbildern und Strategien verankert haben, sind andere noch auf der Suche nach Orientierung. Und das ist ok. Das Hochschulsystem ist komplex, gleichzeitig starr und flexibel und ein Nebeneinander von Tradition und Innovation. Unser Angebot: Die definitive Definition digitaler Souveränität.

The post Digitale Souveränität: Die definitive Definition appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.
full_text:
Digitale Souveränität: Die definitive Definition

Christoph Koitka-Fieke

Hochschulrektorenkonferenz, Referent für IT & Technologie

Uwe Reckzeh-Stein

Hochschulrektorenkonferenz, Referent

Wie werden wir digital souverän, und was heißt das – eigentlich klar so weit, oder? Nein, für die meisten ist es das noch nicht. Während die einen schon eine feste Definition in ihren Zielbildern und Strategien verankert haben, sind andere noch auf der Suche nach Orientierung. Und das ist okay. Das Hochschulsystem ist komplex, gleichzeitig starr und flexibel und ein Nebeneinander von Tradition und Innovation. Unser Angebot: Die definitive Definition digitaler Souveränität.

Überall stellen sich derzeit Hochschulentscheider:innen, Informatik- und Datenexpert:innen und viele weitere Stakeholder die Frage der Digitalen Souveränität.

Was bisher fehlt, ist eine gemeinsame Definition. Was also ist Digitale Souveränität?

Ist sie in greifbarer Nähe, wenn sich der letzte Tech-Gigant aus dem Hochschulsystem verabschiedet hat?

Sind wir digital souverän, wenn alle Kanzler:innen, CIOs und Rektor:innen entsprechende Software kennen und für ihre Hochschule flächendeckend einführen – vielleicht sogar im Verbund, mit weise geteilten Verantwortlichkeiten?

Wenn Forschung, Verwaltung und Lehre nur noch Open Source nutzen: Ist die Digitale Souveränität dann erreicht?

Oder sogar: Alles davon, am besten jetzt, am besten gleichzeitig? Leichtes Nicken bei den Lesenden: Ja, das wäre wahrscheinlich nicht schlecht.

Denn die Zeit drängt, das weiß man nicht nur bei der Gesellschaft für Informatik, wo besonders engagiert darauf hingewiesen wird.

Wer sagt uns jetzt, was wir tun sollen? Wie kommen wir gemeinsam dahin? Beim Hochschulforum Digitalisierung haben wir auch keine schlüsselfertige Lösung oder gar die „definitive Definition Digitaler Souveränität“ im Ärmel. Trotzdem würden wir unser Versprechen aus der Überschrift gern einlösen.

Der definitiven Definition nähern wir uns deswegen aus den verschiedenen Perspektiven an, die das Thema bietet.

Souverän ist, wer zwischen Alternativen wählen und diese Wahl auch wieder revidieren kann. Dafür müssen Verträge, Datenformate und Schnittstellen einen Wechsel zulassen, statt über Lizenzmodelle und Campus-Deals ganze Ökosysteme festzuschreiben. Pragmatische Souveränität heißt nicht, auf kommerzielle Anbieter zu verzichten, sondern die Bedingungen so zu gestalten, dass man jederzeit gehen könnte.

Leitfragen: Was würde es kosten, morgen zu wechseln, und wer zahlt diesen Preis? Und: Was sind unsere Opportunitätskosten, wenn wir nichts verändern?

Technologische Souveränität betrachtet den gesamten Stack: Hardware, Netze, Rechenzentren, Betriebssysteme, Anwendungen und Schnittstellen. Auf jeder Ebene stellt sich die Frage, wer die Technologie kontrolliert, versteht und verändern kann. Vollständige Autarkie ist weder realistisch noch sinnvoll, entscheidend ist, kritische Abhängigkeiten zu kennen und mit offenen Standards, Open Source und europäischen Infrastrukturen gezielt gegenzusteuern.

Leitfrage: Welche Abhängigkeiten sind unvermeidbar, welche selbst gewählt und welche kritisch?

Umstellungen, die nicht gut begleitet werden, gehen zu Lasten derjenigen, die in ihrer täglichen Arbeit auf die vom Arbeitgeber ausgegebene Hard- und Software angewiesen sind. Besonders in Verwaltung und Bibliotheken treffen neue Systeme auf komplexe Prozesse und Strukturen, die teilweise seit Jahrzehnten verankert sind. Die Lösung sind kollaborative und partizipative Change-Prozesse für Media & Data Literacy, die Beschäftigte früh einbinden und Qualifizierung von Anfang an mitdenken.

Leitfrage: Wer muss was können, damit ein Wechsel nicht zur Überforderung wird?

Hochschulen erzeugen Daten in enormer Breite, von Forschungs- über Lern- und Prüfungsdaten bis zu Personal- und Verwaltungsdaten. Datensouveränität heißt, über Speicherort, Zugriff, Nutzung und Weitergabe selbst zu entscheiden, und zwar rechtlich, technisch und organisatorisch. Heikel wird es überall dort, wo Plattformen Nutzungsdaten auswerten oder Inhalte in das Training von KI-Modellen fließen, etwa bei Learning Analytics oder Prompts in KI-Chatbots.

Leitfrage: Könnten wir unsere Daten morgen vollständig und nutzbar zurückholen, und wissen wir, wer sie heute nutzt?

Hier wird es philosophisch und politikwissenschaftlich: Digitale Souveränität ist im föderalen Hochschulsystem immer ein Aushandlungsprozess zwischen Wissenschaftler:innen, Hochschulen und Ländern. Die individuelle Freiheit der einzelnen Wissenschaftler:innen und die Freiheit von Forschung und Lehre dürfen dabei nicht eingeschränkt werden. Dennoch wird das Gesamtsystem nur souveräner, wenn Einzelne an bestimmten Stellen auf eigene Gestaltungsmöglichkeiten verzichten.

Leitfragen: Wie erarbeiten wir konsensual verbindliche Standards und ein gemeinsames Zielbild? Wo hilft die Freiheit einzelner Personen und Hochschulen, und wo ist es effizient, zum Wohle aller auf eigene Gestaltungsmöglichkeiten zu verzichten?

Der Weg führt über Verbünde und Shared Services, getragen von verlässlicher Governance, fairen Kostenmodellen, guter Kommunikation und Vertrauen.

Eine einzelne Hochschule hat gegenüber globalen Konzernen kaum Verhandlungsmacht und übernimmt Vertragsbedingungen meist, wie sie kommen. Ambienta Sgr, società di investimento fondata da Nino Tronchetti Provera e focalizzata sulla sostenibilità, ha acquisito, tramite il fondo Ambienta IV, le aziende norvegesi BioMarine, Flatsetsund Engineering (Fls), Smir e P/F GroAqua Group, quest’ultima delle isole Faroe: quattro realtà attive nelle tecnologie avanzate per l’acquacoltura.

Nasce così una piattaforma industriale che integra le competenze complementari delle quattro società: dalle soluzioni per la tutela della salute dei pesci e l’ottimizzazione dell’alimentazione, dalle attrezzature essenziali per la gestione degli allevamenti, fino ai sistemi per il trattamento degli scarti.

Questo primo nucleo di società pone le basi del progetto di Ambienta di creare un operatore di riferimento nei Paesi Nordici capace di promuovere l’innovazione nell’acquacoltura sostenibile. Grazie all’ampiezza dell’offerta e alle competenze delle quattro società, il gruppo potrà supportare gli allevatori nella riduzione del loro impatto ambientale, estendendo l’applicazione delle proprie soluzioni a diverse specie e aree geografiche.

Milena Torciano, Partner di Ambienta, ha commentato: «L’acquacoltura è una delle fonti di proteine animali più efficienti nell’utilizzo delle risorse e riteniamo possa svolgere un ruolo fondamentale nel soddisfare il fabbisogno alimentare di una popolazione in costante crescita, nel rispetto dei limiti del pianeta. BioMarine, FLS, Smir e GroAqua esprimono appieno le caratteristiche delle aziende a forte contenuto tecnologico in cui intendiamo investire».

Sverre Taknes, ceo della piattaforma, ha aggiunto: «Ciascuna di queste quattro società ha costruito la propria posizione di leadership rispondendo alle esigenze concrete degli allevatori, dall’ottimizzazione dell’alimentazione alla gestione dell’ossigeno, dal controllo dei pidocchi di mare alla biosicurezza. Unendo tecnologie complementari e solide competenze di settore, stiamo creando una piattaforma capace di offrire risposte integrate, accelerare l’innovazione e favorire una più ampia adozione di soluzioni ormai consolidate».
